newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU urges UK to keep cow cull, says to review study.
newsitem.headline: EU urges UK to keep cow cull, says to review study.

text.p: European Commission President Jacques Santer pressed Britain on Wednesday to meet its promise to cull an extra 147,000 cattle while pledging to look at new scientific data saying such a cull was not needed.

In parallel to a public speech urging the cull plan be respected, Santer and his fellow Commissioners agreed to have EU vets look at a British study saying the epidemic would die out by the turn of the century regardless of mass cull measures.
The review promise flew in the face of EU farm ministers' rejection of the data during a meeting in Brussels on Tuesday.

Britain reluctantly agreed to a package of measures in June, including the cull of cattle most at risk from the deadly disease, in return for a gradual lifting of the EU-imposed, worldwide ban on its beef exports.
"I do think we should stick to that agreement as formulated by EU leaders," Santer told a news conference at the European Parliament.
Commissioners offered Britain the olive branch of sending the new study to its scientific veterinary committee to see how it might affect things, a senior official told Reuters.

"The committee will decide whether we have to reconsider the data used for the original package. If it's a change to these measures which the UK is proposing it will have to be something which can be put in place immediately," the official said.
The official denied the offer was a political gesture to help London solve its domestic problems over the affair.
"There are no political reasons for sending it to scientists. It is clear that whatever we do has to be based on science."

Britain believes the new data has thrown doubt on the effectiveness of the extra cull, intended to supplement a scheme to slaughter annually around one million cattle over the age of 30 months and to destroy the meat.
An Oxford University report last month suggested that the disease, known medically as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) would disappear within five years without the necessity of an extra cull.
But Santer said the agreed measures should be implemented.

"We should be taking all the necessary steps to eradicate this disease in order to restore consumer confidence and then stabilise markets. Our over-riding concern is the protection of public health," he said.
Irish Prime Minister John Bruton stressed the Irish EU Presidency was committed to ending the beef crisis, which he believed could only be done through joint European action.
"What is clear is that the matter must be solved...on a European basis. The place to do that is at a European Council (summit) and not unilaterally," he told the news conference.
But Britain increasingly believes that the ban is unlikely to be lifted soon, even if the cull is carried out.
British Prime Minister John Major said on Wednesday Britain had made no firm decision yet about scrapping or reducing it.

"I can tell you we will not delay a decision and when we take the decision we will take it on the basis of public health, on the basis of common sense and in the interests of the beef farmer but there are still discussions to be had before that decision can be finalised," Major said on BBC radio.
British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg failed on Tuesday to persuade other farm ministers or the European Commission to reduce the selective slaughter scheme.

On Wednesday, Hogg warned in London that the British parliament would strongly oppose the scheme, which needs parliamentary approval, unless the EU agreed "rapidly and substantially" to proceed with lifting the ban.
The EU banned British beef exports in March after Britain said that there could be a link between BSE and Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease, the deadly human equivalent.
